subChunks.title: International Collaboration & Repository Networks

storyBeats.txt: Ancestors did not stay in one country, Theodora said. They migrated, traded, colonised, were enslaved, fled, and settled wherever they could. The records that document their lives are scattered across archives in dozens of countries, held in institutions that were not designed to communicate with each other.

The professional genealogist who operates only within their national tradition will hit walls that a researcher with international connections can walk through. The researcher in Ireland who knows their Polish colleague. The American researcher who has built a relationship with the state archive in Saxony. These are professional assets as much as technical skills.

International genealogy is also a field where the norms, record systems, and professional standards of other countries differ substantially from what British or American researchers know. Respect for those differences — and curiosity about them — is what separates the globally competent genealogist from the parochial one.

subChunks.hookHtml:
The global genealogical community is interconnected through a web of international organisations, collaborative digitisation projects, cross-border archive partnerships, and shared online platforms. FamilySearch's global microfilm programme has created a repository of records from 110 countries in a single library. Findmypast, Ancestry, MyHeritage, and Geneanet each have strengths in different national record environments. The Genealogical Proof Standard's framework has been adopted across English-speaking traditions, and equivalent standards exist in other languages.

International collaboration — building professional relationships across national genealogical communities, understanding the record systems of multiple countries, and participating in global advocacy for archive access — is increasingly a mark of the professionally mature genealogist. This lesson surveys the landscape and provides the frameworks for effective international practice.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
International Genealogical Organisations

International Federation of Genealogical Organisations (IFGO): The umbrella organisation connecting national genealogical societies worldwide. IFGO facilitates communication between societies, co-ordinates advocacy on access and preservation issues, and maintains a directory of member societies. Member societies include APG (US), Society of Genealogists (UK), Genealogical Society of Ireland, Genealogical Society of South Africa, and hundreds more.

International Commission for the Accreditation of Professional Genealogists (ICAPGen): Accredits genealogists in specific geographic specialisms through examination. Specialists exist for German, Scandinavian, Eastern European, Latin American, and other record environments. Their directory is the best starting point for finding a specialist researcher in a specific national context.

ISOGG (International Society of Genetic Genealogy): Co-ordinates genetic genealogy standards and education globally. The ISOGG Wiki (isogg.org) is the most comprehensive global reference for DNA genealogy methodology.

Key International Archive Portals

Most national archive systems have developed online portals providing access to finding aids and, increasingly, digital images:

  • TNA Discovery (discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk) — UK, as discussed throughout this course
  • Archivportal-D (archivportal-d.de) — German federal and state archives
  • PARES (pares.mcu.es) — Spanish state archives including AGI (colonial records)
  • Archives Portal Europe (archivesportaleurope.net) — cross-European finding aid aggregator, covering 30+ countries
  • ANOM (anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr) — French colonial archives
  • Arkiv Digital (arkivdigital.se) — Swedish church records and civil registration
  • Matricula Online (data.matricula-online.eu) — Central European Catholic parish registers (Austria, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland)
  • FamilySearch (familysearch.org) — 110-country microfilm programme; the single most important cross-national genealogical resource

Cross-Border Research Collaboration

For research in unfamiliar national record environments, professional collaboration is often the most efficient approach. Strategies include: contracting an ICAPGen-accredited specialist; joining national genealogical societies in countries of research interest (most welcome overseas members; their newsletters and journals contain expertise unavailable elsewhere); attending specialist institutes (Deutschen Genealogentag, German national genealogy congress; Scandinavian Genealogy Institute summer courses); and building informal relationships with researchers who specialise in specific national archives.

The BIFHSGO (British Isles Family History Society of Greater Ottawa) and equivalent diaspora societies are particularly valuable: they bring together North American researchers whose interests intersect with UK/Irish records, creating natural networks for cross-border collaboration.

Diaspora Genealogy and International Research Ethics

Much international genealogical research involves diaspora communities — descendants of migrants who need access to records in countries their ancestors left. This context creates ethical considerations: records held in the country of origin may be subject to that country's privacy and access laws, which differ significantly from UK/US law; communities have their own relationships to their records and their own norms around research and disclosure; and the political history of some regions (partition, conquest, colonial administration) means that record access can be politically sensitive.

Professional international genealogists engage with these realities rather than ignoring them. Working in Polish Jewish genealogy requires understanding the Holocaust memorial organisations' protocols. Working in South Asian genealogy requires engaging with the India Office Records' access conditions. Working in Indigenous records requires understanding tribal sovereignty and the community's own protocols for accessing and sharing genealogical information.

Advocacy for International Archive Access

Many archives impose unreasonable access restrictions — decades-long restrictions on modern civil registration, fees that make research unaffordable, restrictions on photography, or simply inadequate digitisation. Professional genealogical organisations advocate for improved access, typically through: lobbying national archive services; submitting evidence to government inquiries; partnering with archives on digitisation projects; and publicly celebrating improvements in access to increase political pressure for further change.

The Society of Genealogists, APG, and national societies in many countries have active advocacy programmes. Participating in these efforts is a professional contribution that benefits the entire research community, including the next generation of genealogists.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why genealogical research often requires knowing about archives and record systems in other countries — and what professional genealogists do to overcome the language and access barriers.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A client wants to trace their family from a small town in the former German Empire (now part of modern Poland) before emigration to the US in 1902. They have the emigrant's name and approximate birth year (c.1878) and know the town name. Identify: (1) the key international resources you would use; (2) the specialist credentials you would look for if you needed to refer to an external expert; (3) the language and access challenges you would anticipate; and (4) the first three records you would seek.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Key international resources: FamilySearch for German church records (extensive microfilm programme for Prussian provinces); Archivportal-D for finding aids to the relevant state archive (the town, now in Poland, means records may be at the Archiwum Państwowe — Polish state archive — for the relevant voivodeship); Matricula Online for Catholic parish registers if the family was Catholic (covering former German areas now in Poland); FamilySearch Wiki for Germany/Poznan area records; GenTeam for Austrian and Eastern European records if applicable; Ahnen Forscher and Genealogy.net for German resources.

(2) Specialist credentials: ICAPGen Accredited Genealogists (AG) specialising in German records; also consider researchers listed in the professional directories of the Deutschen Genealogenverbandes (German Genealogical Association) or the Arbeitsgemeinschaft Genealogie. For Polish-held records, the Polskie Towarzystwo Genealogiczne (Polish Genealogical Society, ptg.net.pl) directory lists Polish researchers.

(3) Language and access challenges: Records created in the Prussian/German Empire era will be in German (and possibly Latin for older church records), using Kurrent or Sütterlin script — specific handwriting styles that require specialist palaeographic training. The archive holding the records may be in Poland and correspondence may require Polish-language communication. Access may require in-person visits or paid researcher agents.

(4) First three records: (a) US arrival passenger manifest — likely via NARA or Ancestry; will confirm full name, exact origin location (specific village), and possibly nearest relative in origin country. (b) German church baptism record for c.1878 — FamilySearch or Matricula Online for the relevant parish; will give parents' names. (c) Auswanderungslisten (emigration registers) — German states kept emigration records; these may give the emigrant's destination, age, and occupation.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: A genealogical society is considering a formal partnership with a foreign archive to digitise and index a collection of records of significant genealogical interest. Identify: (1) what an appropriate partnership agreement might include; (2) what advocacy arguments would persuade the archive to participate; (3) what quality control standards the digitisation project should follow; and (4) how access to the resulting digital collection would be managed fairly for both the archive's national users and the society's international members.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Partnership agreement elements: Intellectual property — who owns the digital images (typically the archive retains ownership of the original records and their digital surrogates; the society may hold copyright in its indexing or transcription work); access — what access conditions will apply to the digital collection and for how long; quality standards — the agreement should specify minimum resolution, file format, metadata requirements, and verification standards; funding — who bears the digitisation cost, and is there any revenue sharing for access fees or future licensing; promotion — both parties agree to credit each other in publicity; term and renewal — how long the partnership lasts and what happens at the end.

(2) Advocacy arguments: Increased visibility for the archive's collections internationally; reduced handling pressure on fragile originals (digitisation reduces the need for in-person access); potential for the society's index to bring new researchers to the archive's holdings; demonstrated best-practice digitisation at no cost to the archive; potential grant funding available for digitisation projects with an international partner (Heritage Lottery Fund, Europeana Aggregation grants).

(3) Quality control standards: Minimum 400 dpi for text documents; TIFF masters retained; JPEG or PDF/A for access copies; metadata per file including provenance, date digitised, and equipment; double-keying for transcription indexing; sample verification against originals; and a defined standard for what constitutes an acceptable transcription (following an agreed style guide).

(4) Fair access management: Access should be non-discriminatory — the collection should be available to researchers regardless of nationality or society membership, at most with a reasonable registration requirement. If access fees are charged, they should be set at a level that does not exclude researchers from lower-income countries. Consider a tiered access model: free access to the index; small fee for digital image access; depositing a copy of the digital collection with both the archive and the society ensures long-term preservation independent of either organisation's continued involvement.
learningObjectives: Identify the principal international genealogical organisations and their functions (IFGO, ICAPGen, ISOGG).
Describe the key international archive portals (PARES, Archives Portal Europe, Matricula Online, FamilySearch) and their geographic coverage.
Design a cross-border research strategy for a specific international genealogical problem, including specialist referral and language/access considerations.
Explain the ethical dimensions of diaspora genealogy and international research involving Indigenous or minority communities.
commonMistakes: Assuming FamilySearch covers all national records equally — coverage varies significantly by country and record type.
Not checking whether records now in Poland but created during the German Empire era require German (not Polish) language skills and Kurrent palaeography.
Ignoring community protocols when researching Indigenous or minority genealogy in international contexts.
Treating archive access terms as fixed rather than as advocacy targets — professional societies can and do influence policy.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly identifies international resources appropriate to the specific national record environment.
Demonstrates awareness of language and script challenges in international research and how to address them.
Engages with ethical dimensions of diaspora and minority genealogy with appropriate cultural awareness.
Partnership agreement design addresses intellectual property, access, quality, and long-term sustainability.

questions.questionHtml: What is the Archives Portal Europe (archivesportaleurope.net)?
options: A digitised collection of all European genealogical records
A cross-European finding aid aggregator providing a single search interface for archives in 30+ European countries
The European equivalent of the National Archives in the UK
A subscription database for European civil registration records
questions.correctAnswer: A cross-European finding aid aggregator providing a single search interface for archives in 30+ European countries
questions.explanationHtml: Archives Portal Europe aggregates finding aid descriptions from national archives across Europe, providing a single search interface. It does not host the records themselves but directs researchers to the repositories that hold them — an essential first step in identifying where records are held for a specific country or region.

questions.questionHtml: You are researching ancestors from a small town that was in the German Empire in 1890 but is now in Poland. The church records for the town were created in German. What specialist skill is most critical for reading these records?
options: Knowledge of Kurrent or Sütterlin German script
questions.correctAnswer: Knowledge of Kurrent or Sütterlin German script
questions.explanationHtml: Church and civil records created in the German Empire were typically written in Kurrent (earlier) or Sütterlin (later 19th/early 20th century) — German cursive scripts that differ substantially from modern handwriting and from the English Secretary Hand. Reading these records requires specific German palaeography training, regardless of whether the records are now held in a Polish archive.

questions.questionHtml: Why is it important for genealogists researching Indigenous records internationally to engage with the relevant community's own protocols, rather than applying standard genealogical access approaches?
options: Because Indigenous records are held in national archives and require government permission to access
Because tribal sovereignty means Indigenous nations are sovereign entities with their own legal frameworks and cultural protocols that take precedence over national archive access norms
Because Indigenous genealogical research requires DNA testing, which is culturally inappropriate
Because Indigenous records are unavailable to non-tribal researchers under all circumstances
questions.correctAnswer: Because tribal sovereignty means Indigenous nations are sovereign entities with their own legal frameworks and cultural protocols that take precedence over national archive access norms
questions.explanationHtml: Indigenous nations in North America, Australasia, and elsewhere are recognised sovereign entities with their own governance, legal systems, and cultural protocols. This sovereignty means that accessing records about tribal members and their genealogy requires engaging with tribal authorities and their specific protocols — not simply applying national archive access rules. Ignoring this distinction is both legally problematic and culturally disrespectful.
